title: Looking back: the ragas

segments.voice: Yesterday, the close of Sikh thought: God, the self, how to live and the world. Your line was the idea that stayed. Who did you tell about yours? Day one thousand four hundred twenty.

Some songs belong to a time of day. A lullaby at noon sounds wrong. A wedding song at a funeral would be unbearable. The Sikh tradition built it into the scripture itself. So as this year of the ways of the Guru begins to close, the looking back starts here, with the sound under the words. Over the year you've met hymns of praise, of longing, of warning, of joy. Hymn after hymn came with a heading that named its raga before anything else. Today, before looking back at what the Gurus said, a look back at how it was meant to be heard.
screen: `A LULLABY AT NOON SOUNDS WRONG.` → `THE YEAR BEGINS TO CLOSE.` → `HOW IT WAS MEANT TO BE HEARD.`

segments.voice: First, the headings. You met this a week ago: after the opening prayers, the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raga. The hymns you've heard this year sat under raga names, like a door you walk through before you hear a word. Second, a raga is a mood. Musicians in the tradition speak of each one having its own color and its own hour. In Sikh practice, Asa di Var is sung in the early morning. Tradition links Basant with spring and Malar with the rains. The Word doesn't change, but it arrives dressed for the moment. Third, the moods are honest. The Granth doesn't stay cheerful. In Raag Tukhari, Guru Nanak's song of the months walks through the year as a bride longing for her beloved: the heat, the rain, the cold, each month its own ache, until union comes. Longing gets its own music. So does warning, so does celebration. Nobody is asked to fake a mood they're not in. Fourth, one Word, many moods. That may be the real lesson of the ragas as the year closes. The same Name is sung in grief and in joy, at dawn and at night, in spring and in the rains. There's a raga for whatever state you walk in with. Which means there's no mood that has to be fixed before coming near the Word. You bring the mood. The music meets it.
screen: `HYMNS UNDER A RAGA'S NAME.` · `A RAGA IS A MOOD AND AN HOUR.` · `TUKHARI: THE SONG OF THE MONTHS.` · `ONE WORD, MANY MOODS.` · then, large: `MANY MOODS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to your raga. Settle, and breathe. First, name your mood right now, honestly, in one word: tired, hopeful, restless, sad, light. Don't correct it. Then ask which hour it belongs to: dawn, noon, dusk or deep night. And which season: spring, the rains, the heat, the cold. Let that hour and season settle around you, the way a raga heading sits over a hymn. Breathe inside it. Notice whether the mood shifts, or just feels accompanied. If you pray, you can bring the mood as it is, in that hour. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. At the year's close, the ragas: hymns under a mood's name, one Word sung for every state you're in. Today's word.
Your line: many moods. Today, when your mood changes, name it, and ask what kind of music it needs, instead of what kind of fixing. Day one thousand four hundred twenty.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras, ragis (kirtan musicians) sing hymns in the raga named at their head, and Sikh practice sets particular hymns, such as Asa di Var in the morning, for particular times.
